visual_format: chart (10 by 10 icon array) plus statement card, 2 slides
visual_text: By discharge, 60 (about 17 in 100) said they could no longer control their bladder
Acute medical patients aged 70 and over, one Israeli teaching hospital. Reported by the patient at discharge; not followed up afterwards.
Said they could no longer control their bladder at discharge: 60 of 352
Each icon stands for about 3.5 people (100 icons for 352)
Zisberg et al., J Am Geriatr Soc, 2011
Pads or a catheter were linked with new leaking
Using pads or a catheter for most of the stay was linked with new incontinence at discharge, compared with using the toilet, after allowing for age, illness severity, mobility and memory.
This shows a link. It does not show that pads or a catheter caused the leaking.
Frailer people are more likely to be given pads (Danish study of about 2,000 older patients).
Our judgement: help people to the toilet by default, and ask why when a new 'incontinent' record appears.
Zisberg et al., J Am Geriatr Soc, 2011; Larsen et al., Int J Nurs Stud Adv, 2023
alt_text: Icon array of 100 person icons standing for 352 older hospital patients who were all continent on admission. 17 icons are filled orange with a ring, the rest are teal outlines. By discharge 60 of 352, about 17 in 100, said they could no longer control their bladder. Acute medical patients aged 70 and over, one Israeli hospital.

Text card. Pads or a catheter for most of the stay were linked with new incontinence at discharge, after allowing for age, illness, mobility and memory. It shows a link, not cause; frailer people get pads more often. Our judgement, in a mint panel: help people to the toilet by default and ask why when a new incontinent record appears.
